svg.desc: candidate number: 48; slug: data-mined-qui-tam,-sec-&-irs-whistleblower-analytics; title: Data-Mined Qui Tam, SEC & IRS Whistleblower Analytics; category: Forensic whistleblower analytics; production stage: approved_master; scores: revenue potential: 24; profit margin potential: 24; team efficiency: 20; startup accessibility: 12; automation potential: 12; dimension max: revenue potential: 25; profit margin potential: 25; team efficiency: 20; startup accessibility: 15; automation potential: 15; total score: 92; tier label: Elite Small-Team Cash Machine; evidence confidence: High; uncertainty band: ±3 pts; uncertainty bounds: low: 89; high: 95; uncertainty note: Editorial sensitivity band, not a statistical interval. Cross-correlating public CMS Part B/D billing, Open Payments, SAM.gov procurement, and import manifests funds a 3-person forensic pod via relator-firm retainers plus 15%–30% statutory whistleblower awards.; economics: gross revenue range: $95,000–$880,000 USD annually; retained revenue range: $95,000–$880,000 USD annually; retained share: 1.0; net profit margin range: 32–58%; retained profit margin range: 32–58%; owner net profit potential: $30,400–$510,400 USD annually, before personal taxes and reinvestment; startup capital range: $10,000–$45,000 USD; monthly opex range: $1,500–$9,500 USD; time to first deal: 4–12 months; automation coverage: 0.83; typical team size: full time including owner: 1; contractors: 2; total people: 3; includes contractors note: Headcount includes the working owner and recurring contractors as people, not FTE equivalents. Contractors may be part-time. Scaled scenario adds one employee and one contractor; external vendor workforces are not counted as internal team members.; revenue basis: Paid forensic litigation-support retainers from plaintiff/relator law firms plus realized net statutory relator/whistleblower award shares; cost basis: Annual net margins include operating expenses and non-owner labor; monthly opex is fixed/semi-fixed overhead only. No owner salary is deducted. Capital needs may grow beyond startup range.; estimate status: Illustrative assumptions; not verified earnings data; scenarios: conservative: annual gross revenue usd: 95000; annual retained revenue usd: 95000; net profit margin pct: 32; retained profit margin pct: 32.0; annual owner net profit usd: 30400; full time including owner: 1; contractors: 2; total people: 3; assumption: Illustrative established-operation run rate, not first-year earnings. Margin includes operating costs and non-owner labor; owner labor is not separately compensated. Scale requires additional demand, working capital and delivery capacity.; automation levers: CMS Part B/D, Open Payments & import-manifest outlier engine; FOIA & primary-source corroboration dossier builder; Relator-counsel litigation-support & seal-compliance tracker; key risks: 31 U.S.C. § 3730(e)(4) public-disclosure bar dismissals; Multi-year DOJ seal investigations & non-intervention; Strict court-seal breach disqualifying relator share; regulatory notes: File all False Claims Act qui tam complaints exclusively through licensed relator counsel under strict 31 U.S.C. § 3730(b)(2) court seal, and route SEC Form TCR / IRS Form 211 filings through counsel.; Pair long-tail statutory relator upside with recurring B2B forensic data-analytics retainers so operating cashflow never depends on uncollected seal dockets.; track ids: track_1; track_2; track labels: Asymmetric & Data-Arbitrage Plays; Grey-Zone Growth & Traffic Arbitrage; plays: id: fca_qui_tam_and_sec_whistleblower_forensic_analytics; inputs: Lawfully obtained procurement, payment, grant, corporate-filing, enforcement, and pricing datasets with acquisition dates, source URLs, applicable use rights, immutable snapshots, transformation code, and a documented separation of public records from any authorized nonpublic evidence.; Counsel-defined investigative hypotheses identifying the relevant payment or securities/tax theory, responsible actors, transaction dates, representations, materiality, estimated loss, alternative explanations, and unresolved evidentiary gaps.; Written analytics engagement covering scope, ordinary service fees, conflicts, confidentiality, evidence retention, and ownership; separate counsel assessments of FCA public disclosure, original-source status, first-to-file and limitations issues, SEC original-information requirements, and IRS submission eligibility.; mechanism: Sell scoped B2B forensic-analytics retainers to contingency relator firms, producing reproducible evidence packages for potential False Claims Act matters under 31 U.S.C. §§ 3729–3730 and distinct SEC or IRS whistleblower pathways under 15 U.S.C. § 78u-6 and 26 U.S.C. § 7623. Public-data anomalies alone do not establish a knowingly false, material claim or satisfy Rule 9(b); FCA public-disclosure and original-source analysis differs from the SEC's potential recognition of qualifying independent analysis. Treat service revenue as the operating business and any personally eligible whistleblower award as separate, contingent, potentially multi-year proceeds rather than a purchased claim, promised recovery, or share of counsel's legal fees.; metrics: Collected retainer and milestone revenue minus analyst labor, data licensing, expert review, secure storage, and rework; track receivable days and client concentration without booking speculative awards as earned service revenue.; Evidence quality: reproducible transaction coverage, precision on manually reviewed anomalies, documented alternative explanations, and the share of allegations supported by claim-specific facts rather than aggregate correlations.; Program-specific contingent recovery register: FCA shares generally 15–25% with government intervention or 25–30% without, subject to statutory exceptions; SEC awards generally 10–30% of collected sanctions in qualifying actions exceeding $1 million; IRS § 7623(b) generally 15–30% subject to its monetary, taxpayer-income, and other requirements.; name: Public-Data Forensic Analytics and Relator Litigation-Support Desk; platform risks: detection metric: Measure unresolved statutory-element gaps, unsupported claim assertions, source-provenance exceptions, and matters lacking a documented program-specific assessment by counsel.; failure mode: A compelling statistical pattern is sold as an award-eligible case despite public-disclosure restrictions, insufficient claim-specific facts, or a mismatch between the evidence and the selected whistleblower program.; fallback: Narrow the deliverable to supported forensic findings, preserve exculpatory evidence, and pursue further lawful corroboration only within the engagement; stop unsupported allegations and retain collected service-fee economics separately from any abandoned award thesis.; impact: Dismissal, award denial, wasted litigation expense, confidentiality exposure, and impaired client relationships; paid analytics work does not itself establish relator standing or award eligibility.; trigger: The material is already publicly disclosed or known to authorities, the analyst contributes no qualifying independent analysis or original-source knowledge, or counsel cannot connect anomalies to the required statutory elements.; track id: track_1; workflow: 1. Select a narrow, counsel-approved hypothesis and reproduce the underlying transactions from preserved source data; document methodology, false-positive controls, lawful access, and contrary evidence without accessing restricted systems or soliciting privileged material.; 2. Build a transaction-level evidence matrix linking alleged conduct to identifiable claims, statements, actors, dates, knowledge indicators, and materiality; have counsel test Rule 9(b) particularity under the governing circuit and assess FCA public-disclosure and original-source issues before characterizing a matter as actionable.; 3. Deliver the paid forensic report and reproducible workpapers independently of any award outcome; counsel selects the appropriate pathway, including an FCA complaint initially filed under seal with statutory government disclosures, an SEC TCR submission, or an IRS Form 211, rather than treating the programs as interchangeable.; 4. Maintain controlled litigation support, evidence updates, and a docket of counsel-managed deadlines; respect the FCA's initial statutory seal period of at least 60 days and any court-granted extensions, which can extend for years, while forecasting operations from collected retainers rather than expected awards.; id: public_record_api_intelligence; track id: track_1; name: Public-Record & API Intelligence; mechanism: Ingest fragmented county dockets, probate registries, unclaimed property ledgers, and public APIs to surface uncontested claims or high-intent B2B triggers before manual competitors.; inputs: Court & probate dockets; State controller ledgers; Public licensing & entity APIs; workflow: Poll and normalize county/state record releases on an automated cadence; Cross-match entity/kinship/lien records and filter by minimum net fee threshold; Route verified dossiers into compliant outreach and claim execution; metrics: Cost per verified lead; Docket-to-contact latency (hours); Net recovery / conversion rate; platform risks: failure mode: Portal rate-limiting or CAPTCHA gating; trigger: High-frequency automated polling against county or agency web portals; impact: Delayed lead ingestion or temporary IP block on target registry; detection metric: HTTP 429/403 rate and daily record ingestion delta; fallback: Switch to scheduled bulk FOIA/public-record exports, official data feeds, and low-frequency cached queues; id: sec_edgar_8k_vendor_trigger_arbitrage; track id: track_1; name: SEC Form 8-K, Form D & C-Suite Turnover Trigger Arbitrage; mechanism: Parse SEC EDGAR real-time RSS/JSON feeds for Form D (private Reg D capital raises) and Form 8-K (Item 5.02 C-suite departures, Item 1.01 material agreements, Item 2.01 M&A closings) to trigger sub-hour executive outreach before commercial databases update.; inputs: SEC EDGAR real-time Submissions API & Form D / Form 8-K XML feeds; Automated filing parser extracting raise amounts, executive names, & signatory contacts; Enterprise recruiting, specialty finance, & B2B agency deal-routing desk; workflow: Ingest SEC EDGAR filings within seconds of publication using a compliant User-Agent header (<=10 requests/second); Extract Form D issuers raising $2M–$50M (who immediately deploy capital on hiring, growth agencies, and software) and Form 8-K executive transitions; Deliver tailored briefings to the filing officers and route warm introductions to executive search firms, enterprise software resellers, and B2B agencies; metrics: EDGAR publication-to-enrichment latency (seconds); Form D / 8-K executive response rate vs. cold baseline (3–5x lift); Retainer and placement referral fees generated per 100 filings; platform risks: failure mode: SEC EDGAR automated-access block or Reg D general-solicitation confusion; trigger: Exceeding SEC EDGAR's 10-requests-per-second fair-access limit or omitting the mandatory contact User-Agent header; impact: Temporary IP block by Akamai/SEC infrastructure; detection metric: Request rate strictly <=5 req/sec with compliant User-Agent and zero HTTP 403 responses; fallback: Enforce token-bucket rate limiting at 5 req/sec and mirror SEC nightly bulk zip archives for historical lookbacks; id: customs_first_sale_rule_valuation_arbitrage; track id: track_1; name: CBP "First-Sale Rule" (19 CFR § 152.103) Multi-Tier Customs Valuation Arbitrage; mechanism: Restructuring multi-tiered import supply chains under the US Court of Appeals *Nissho Iwai* 'First Sale Rule' so US importers legally declare the lower factory-to-middleman transaction price ($8) for US Customs duty and tariff calculation rather than the middleman-to-US-importer invoice price ($18)—slashing annual tariff cash outflows by 35–55% across $10M–$250M+ in imported merchandise.; inputs: US Customs bill-of-lading and HTS duty-spend intelligence identifying mid-market importers paying $1M–$20M/yr in duties via trading companies; Three-party contract, factory cost-sheet, and arm's-length transfer-pricing documentation templates satisfying CBP *Nissho Iwai* criteria; Licensed customs brokerage and trade-attorney opinion pipeline; workflow: Identify US importers purchasing finished goods through Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwanese, or European trading intermediaries or sourcing agents; Audit the two-tier transaction chain to confirm (1) bona fide sale from factory to middleman, (2) clear designation for US export at factory order, and (3) arm's-length pricing; Implement compliant multi-tier invoicing and ERP documentary trails so the customs broker declares the factory's First-Sale price on CBP Form 7501 instead of the middleman's marked-up invoice; Collect a 25–35% contingency fee on all prospective and retroactive (Post-Summary Correction / Protest) duty reductions realized by the importer; metrics: Percentage reduction in declared customs dutiable value (typically 30–50%); Annualized cash tariff savings ($300k–$5M+/yr per importer) and retroactive PSC refund recovery ($); CBP CF-28/CF-29 Request for Information audit survival rate (100% documentary compliance); platform risks: failure mode: CBP disallowance of First-Sale valuation during a CF-28 Request for Information audit; trigger: Related-party factory/middleman entities failing to prove arm's-length profit margins or refusing to disclose factory commercial invoices; impact: Re-assessment of duties on the second-sale price plus interest; detection metric: Annual pre-audit verification of factory commercial invoices, bank wire proofs, and OECD transfer-pricing benchmark studies; fallback: Store encrypted factory invoices in a confidential customs-broker escrow vault (so the US buyer never sees the middleman's margin, while CBP auditors have full access) and back every program with a formal customs-counsel opinion letter; id: gsa_municipal_set_aside_facility_ghost_brokering; track id: track_1; name: GSA & Municipal Set-Aside Pass-Through Facility Ghost-Brokering; mechanism: Match eligible facility-service primes with disclosed qualified subcontractors and earn documented coordination fees; opaque pass-throughs and false set-aside eligibility are excluded.; inputs: GSA and municipal facility solicitations; Prime eligibility and subcontracting-limit documentation; Licensed local vendor bids and capacity records; workflow: 1. Screen solicitations for service scope, eligibility, and permitted subcontracting; 2. Verify the prime performs required work and disclose broker and subcontractor roles; 3. Submit priced delivery plans with genuine vendor commitments and required certifications; 4. Track service acceptance, payroll obligations, and authorized fee payments against contract terms; metrics: Compliant bids accepted (%); Net coordination margin per contract; On-time service acceptance rate; platform risks: failure mode: Set-aside eligibility protest or prohibited pass-through finding; trigger: Inaccurate certification or subcontracting beyond contract limits; impact: Termination, repayment demands, or debarment exposure; detection metric: Unverified certifications and subcontracted work share versus permitted limits; fallback: Withdraw noncompliant bids and operate as a disclosed subcontractor on unrestricted work; id: government_rfp_subcontractor_brokerage; track id: track_1; name: SAM.gov / Municipal RFP Scraping & Prime-Subcontractor Spread Arbitrage; mechanism: Scrape federal SAM.gov, state procurement portals, and municipal bid boards for low-bid-density service solicitations (janitorial, grounds, courier, translation, IT staffing), pairing compliant proposal automation with vetted local fulfillment subcontractors for a 15–30% management spread.; inputs: SAM.gov Contract Opportunities API & state/municipal e-procurement feeds; Historical FPDS award pricing benchmark database; Vetted local subcontractor network with FAR limitation-on-subcontracting compliance; workflow: Screen daily federal, state, and municipal RFPs/RFQs with <3 historical bidders and clear unit-price schedules; Benchmark winning historical unit rates via FPDS/FOIA award records and lock in binding back-to-back quotes from insured local operators; Submit compliant bid packages and manage billing, insurance, and QA reporting while retaining a 15–30% prime-management or authorized broker spread; metrics: Bid-to-award win rate (%) on low-competition solicitations; Net prime-to-subcontractor gross margin (15–30% target); Contract renewal / option-year retention rate; platform risks: failure mode: FAR 52.219-14 (Limitations on Subcontracting) violation or illegal pass-through scheme; trigger: Bidding small-business set-aside contracts and subcontracting 100% of the work to non-similarly-situated entities without performing required prime share; impact: Contract termination for default, False Claims Act liability, or SAM.gov debarment; detection metric: Subcontracted labor-cost percentage strictly within FAR 52.219-14 limits (<=50% for services unless partnering with similarly situated small businesses); fallback: Bid unrestricted commercial/municipal contracts without set-aside caps, or team exclusively with 'similarly situated entities' under 13 CFR § 125.6; id: hospital_lien_medical_receivables_arbitrage; track id: track_1; name: Out-of-Network Medical Claim & ERISA Appeal Contingency Recovery; mechanism: Partner with surgical centers, air/ground ambulance operators, and specialty clinics to ingest underpaid or denied commercial insurance claims, automating federal No Surprises Act IDR (Independent Dispute Resolution) and ERISA administrative appeals on a 20–35% contingency fee.; inputs: Provider 835/837 EDI remittance & denial feeds (CO-45, CO-50, PR-96 codes); Qualified Payment Amount (QPA) & regional FAIR Health benchmark database; Automated ERISA plan-document demand & Federal IDR portal filing workflow; workflow: Ingest denied and severely underpaid out-of-network commercial claims from specialty medical practices; Cross-reference payer remittances against statutory Open Negotiation windows (30 business days) under the No Surprises Act and ERISA SPD timelines; Generate evidence-backed arbitration briefs and ERISA appeals, collecting 20–35% of the incremental insurer payout above the initial remittance; metrics: Average incremental recovery per arbitrated claim ($1,500–$25,000+); IDR / ERISA appeal win rate vs. initial payer offer (%); Contingency revenue per practice partner per month; platform risks: failure mode: Missed 30-day Open Negotiation / 4-day IDR initiation statutory deadlines or HIPAA breach; trigger: Failing to file within strict federal No Surprises Act business-day windows or handling PHI without a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA); impact: Permanent forfeiture of IDR arbitration eligibility on expired claims or HIPAA compliance penalties; detection metric: 100% BAA execution before EDI ingestion and automated T-minus-5-day statutory deadline alerts; fallback: Enforce HIPAA-compliant encrypted EDI pipelines with signed BAAs and fall back to longer-window ERISA administrative appeals when IDR windows have lapsed; id: section_340b_contract_pharmacy_spread_arbitrage; track id: track_1; name: 340B Contract-Pharmacy & Covered-Entity Drug Price Spread Arbitrage; mechanism: Partnering with HRSA-qualified 340B Covered Entities (Federally Qualified Health Centers, Ryan White clinics, disproportionate-share rural hospitals) to provide turnkey Third-Party Administrator (TPA) split-billing software, specialty contract-pharmacy fulfillment, and tele-referral capture—buying outpatient specialty medications at 25–50%+ statutory 340B discounts while collecting 100% full commercial insurance reimbursement and splitting the multi-thousand-dollar per-script margin via compliant flat administrative/dispensing fees.; inputs: HRSA OPAIS (Office of Pharmacy Affairs Information System) database of Covered Entities and registered contract pharmacies; 340B split-billing / virtual-inventory accumulator software tracking 11-digit NDCs, prescriber NPIs, and patient-eligibility encounters; Licensed specialty/mail-order contract pharmacy network and commercial payer PBMs; workflow: Identify under-monetized 340B Covered Entities (FQHCs, grantees, rural hospitals) with low specialty capture rates in the HRSA OPAIS registry; Deploy split-billing TPA software and mail-order specialty contract-pharmacy infrastructure that captures commercially insured prescriptions written or co-managed by clinic providers; Reimburse the pharmacy at full commercial payer rates ($3,000–$12,000/script) while replenishing drug inventory via the clinic's 340B wholesaler account at $800–$4,000/script; Charge fixed fair-market-value per-dispense administrative, software, and clinical-management fees that capture a major share of the net spread while funding the clinic's safety-net mission; metrics: Captured commercially insured 340B scripts per month per Covered Entity; Gross commercial-to-340B acquisition spread ($1,500–$6,000+) per specialty fill; HRSA audit pass rate (zero duplicate Medicaid discount or diversion findings); platform risks: failure mode: Manufacturer contract-pharmacy restriction policies or HRSA 'patient definition' audit findings; trigger: Drug manufacturers restricting 340B replenishment to a single contract pharmacy unless claims data is submitted, or filling scripts for patients without a documented clinic encounter; impact: Loss of 340B ceiling price on specific NDCs or HRSA repayment liability; detection metric: 100% EHR encounter-to-NPI match verification prior to 340B replenishment accumulation and automated ESP (340B ESP) data submission; fallback: Operate an in-house entity-owned specialty pharmacy location alongside contract pharmacies, automate 340B ESP claims-data uploads to unlock restricted NDCs, and enforce strict EHR encounter gates; id: free_tier_api_waterfall_multiplexing; track id: track_1; name: Multi-Provider Free-Tier API Router & B2B Data-Enrichment Reselling; mechanism: Aggregating 30–60+ distinct B2B data, email-verification, firmographic, DNS, and SERP providers that each offer permanent 'Freemium / Developer Free Tiers' (50–1,000 free lookups/month per provider) behind an intelligent waterfall router with aggressive Postgres caching, selling unified B2B lead enrichment and verification at $99–$499/mo with near-zero upstream API COGS.; inputs: Catalog of 30–60+ B2B contact, firmographic, WHOIS, technographic, and email-verification APIs with recurring free quotas; Deterministic local Postgres/Redis entity cache indexed by domain, LinkedIn URL, and normalized company name; Quota-aware waterfall routing engine with per-provider rate-limit and credit-reset telemetry; workflow: Intercept every incoming B2B enrichment request against the local canonical cache first (eliminating 60–80% of repeat domain/contact lookups at $0 cost); Route cache misses dynamically across the pool of 30+ upstream providers ordered by remaining monthly free-tier quota and field-level accuracy; Normalize disparate provider JSON responses into a single high-confidence schema with verified SMTP handshakes and confidence scores; Persist every newly resolved record into the proprietary local graph so the dataset compounds daily while upstream API spend remains near zero; metrics: Local cache hit rate (%) vs. upstream free-tier quota utilization (%); Effective upstream API cost per 1,000 enriched B2B records ($); Proprietary entity-graph growth rate (net new verified records cached per day); platform risks: failure mode: Upstream providers deprecating free developer tiers or tightening rate limits; trigger: SaaS vendors eliminating free tiers during pricing overhauls or throttling high-concurrency burst requests; impact: Reduced free lookup capacity requiring fallback to paid wholesale tiers or direct scraping; detection metric: Real-time HTTP 429/402 error rate per upstream provider and remaining monthly free-pool runway; fallback: Maintain 40+ interchangeable upstream adapters, prioritize local graph cache hits, and fall back to direct public-web/DNS/MX extraction when free quotas tighten; id: cloud_ai_startup_credit_aggregation_arbitrage; track id: track_1; name: Cloud & LLM Startup Credit Grant Aggregation ($50k–$350k Free Compute Arbitrage); mechanism: Forming clean Delaware/Wyoming micro-SaaS corporate entities enrolled in verified incubator, venture-partner, or founder-perk directories to unlock non-dilutive cloud and frontier LLM startup credit grants ($25k–$350k across AWS Activate, Azure Founders Hub, GCP for Startups, Cloudflare, OpenAI, and Anthropic), eliminating compute COGS for heavy AI data-extraction, scraping, and B2B SaaS products sold at 90–98% cash margins.; inputs: Clean corporate entity registrations, domain workspace, and live product landing/application endpoints; Partnerperk/incubator affiliation tiers (Y Combinator Startup School, Stripe Atlas, Mercury Raise, Microsoft for Startups); Multi-provider LLM and cloud workload router abstracting inference across AWS Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and GCP Vertex; workflow: Provision dedicated vertical micro-SaaS products with live billing, production authentication, and verified corporate domains; Enroll each entity in legitimate startup credit programs to secure $25k–$350k in non-dilutive compute, GPU, and LLM token grants; Route high-volume B2B document parsing, skip-tracing, programmatic content generation, or audio/video transcription workloads across active grant balances; Sell the resulting B2B intelligence, API access, or SaaS subscriptions for hard cash while tracking credit burn and migrating matured workloads to reserved or open-weight self-hosted inference before grant expiration; metrics: Approved non-dilutive compute credit balance ($) per operating entity; Effective cash revenue generated per $1.00 of nominal grant compute consumed; Blended gross margin (%) after grant burn and post-grant unit-economics survival rate; platform risks: failure mode: Cloud provider startup-program audit or credit revocation for linked shell entities or prohibited token reselling; trigger: Reusing identical payment cards, billing addresses, or raw API proxy endpoints across multiple entities without a genuine application layer; impact: Immediate revocation of promotional credits and potential billing-account suspension; detection metric: Zero raw API key proxying; 100% application-layer value-add and isolated corporate/banking governance per product; fallback: Operate genuine standalone vertical SaaS products per entity, never resell raw API keys, and maintain local open-weight (Llama/vLLM/DeepSeek) failover nodes for zero-downtime migration; id: multi_inbox_free_workspace_outbound_clusters; track id: track_2; name: Subsidized / Developer-Tenant Multi-Inbox Cold Outbound Infrastructure; mechanism: Provisioning hundreds of isolated secondary domains across subsidized Microsoft 365 developer/partner tenants, Cloudflare Email Routing, and low-cost SMTP relays—sending strictly 15–25 plain-text emails per inbox per day across 300+ free/subsidized mailboxes to deliver 150,000+ monthly B2B cold emails into primary inboxes without paying $6–$12/seat retail Google Workspace pricing.; inputs: Lookalike secondary domain portfolio with automated SPF, DKIM (2048-bit), DMARC (`p=quarantine`/`reject`), and custom tracking-free MX records; Subsidized M365 partner/developer tenants, Cloudflare Email Routing catch-alls, and distributed SMTP sending nodes; Automated peer-to-peer warmup network and master unibox reply-routing webhook; workflow: Provision 100–300 secondary sending domains and bind 2–3 mailboxes per domain via automated DNS and tenant scripts; Warm every mailbox for 14–21 days with realistic thread-depth conversations before introducing live outbound prospects; Cap daily outbound volume at <=20 zero-link, zero-tracking-pixel plain-text messages per mailbox per day to stay completely beneath ESP volume heuristics; Aggregate all prospect replies into a single unified AI-triaged inbox that books qualified B2B sales calls on pay-per-show or retainer terms; metrics: Primary-inbox placement rate (%) across Gmail and Microsoft 365 seed tests; All-in monthly infrastructure cost per 10,000 delivered plain-text emails ($); Positive reply rate (%) and booked meetings per 1,000 prospects contacted; platform risks: failure mode: Tenant-wide outbound throttling or domain-footprint blacklisting (Spamhaus DBL); trigger: Placing too many domains inside a single tenant, embedding tracking pixels, or exceeding 30 sends/day per mailbox; impact: Tenant suspension or domain-level spam-folder routing; detection metric: Daily seed-list inbox placement (%) and bounce rate (<1.5% hard threshold); fallback: Enforce max 2–3 domains per tenant, strip all open/click tracking pixels, verify 100% of leads via SMTP catch-all checks before sending, and keep hot-standby warmed domains ready for instant swap; platform risks: detection metric: Measure unresolved statutory-element gaps, unsupported claim assertions, source-provenance exceptions, and matters lacking a documented program-specific assessment by counsel.; failure mode: A compelling statistical pattern is sold as an award-eligible case despite public-disclosure restrictions, insufficient claim-specific facts, or a mismatch between the evidence and the selected whistleblower program.; fallback: Narrow the deliverable to supported forensic findings, preserve exculpatory evidence, and pursue further lawful corroboration only within the engagement; stop unsupported allegations and retain collected service-fee economics separately from any abandoned award thesis.; impact: Dismissal, award denial, wasted litigation expense, confidentiality exposure, and impaired client relationships; paid analytics work does not itself establish relator standing or award eligibility.; trigger: The material is already publicly disclosed or known to authorities, the analyst contributes no qualifying independent analysis or original-source knowledge, or counsel cannot connect anomalies to the required statutory elements.; fallback: Bid unrestricted commercial/municipal contracts without set-aside caps, or team exclusively with 'similarly situated entities' under 13 CFR § 125.6; play id: government_rfp_subcontractor_brokerage; play name: SAM.gov / Municipal RFP Scraping & Prime-Subcontractor Spread Arbitrage; track id: track_1; failure mode: Missed 30-day Open Negotiation / 4-day IDR initiation statutory deadlines or HIPAA breach; trigger: Failing to file within strict federal No Surprises Act business-day windows or handling PHI without a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA); impact: Permanent forfeiture of IDR arbitration eligibility on expired claims or HIPAA compliance penalties; detection metric: 100% BAA execution before EDI ingestion and automated T-minus-5-day statutory deadline alerts; fallback: Enforce HIPAA-compliant encrypted EDI pipelines with signed BAAs and fall back to longer-window ERISA administrative appeals when IDR windows have lapsed; play id: hospital_lien_medical_receivables_arbitrage; play name: Out-of-Network Medical Claim & ERISA Appeal Contingency Recovery; track id: track_1; failure mode: Manufacturer contract-pharmacy restriction policies or HRSA 'patient definition' audit findings; trigger: Drug manufacturers restricting 340B replenishment to a single contract pharmacy unless claims data is submitted, or filling scripts for patients without a documented clinic encounter; impact: Loss of 340B ceiling price on specific NDCs or HRSA repayment liability; detection metric: 100% EHR encounter-to-NPI match verification prior to 340B replenishment accumulation and automated ESP (340B ESP) data submission; fallback: Operate an in-house entity-owned specialty pharmacy location alongside contract pharmacies, automate 340B ESP claims-data uploads to unlock restricted NDCs, and enforce strict EHR encounter gates; play id: section_340b_contract_pharmacy_spread_arbitrage; play name: 340B Contract-Pharmacy & Covered-Entity Drug Price Spread Arbitrage; track id: track_1; failure mode: Upstream providers deprecating free developer tiers or tightening rate limits; trigger: SaaS vendors eliminating free tiers during pricing overhauls or throttling high-concurrency burst requests; impact: Reduced free lookup capacity requiring fallback to paid wholesale tiers or direct scraping; detection metric: Real-time HTTP 429/402 error rate per upstream provider and remaining monthly free-pool runway; fallback: Maintain 40+ interchangeable upstream adapters, prioritize local graph cache hits, and fall back to direct public-web/DNS/MX extraction when free quotas tighten; play id: free_tier_api_waterfall_multiplexing; play name: Multi-Provider Free-Tier API Router & B2B Data-Enrichment Reselling; track id: track_1; failure mode: Cloud provider startup-program audit or credit revocation for linked shell entities or prohibited token reselling; trigger: Reusing identical payment cards, billing addresses, or raw API proxy endpoints across multiple entities without a genuine application layer; impact: Immediate revocation of promotional credits and potential billing-account suspension; detection metric: Zero raw API key proxying; 100% application-layer value-add and isolated corporate/banking governance per product; fallback: Operate genuine standalone vertical SaaS products per entity, never resell raw API keys, and maintain local open-weight (Llama/vLLM/DeepSeek) failover nodes for zero-downtime migration; play id: cloud_ai_startup_credit_aggregation_arbitrage; play name: Cloud & LLM Startup Credit Grant Aggregation ($50k–$350k Free Compute Arbitrage); track id: track_1; failure mode: Tenant-wide outbound throttling or domain-footprint blacklisting (Spamhaus DBL); trigger: Placing too many domains inside a single tenant, embedding tracking pixels, or exceeding 30 sends/day per mailbox; impact: Tenant suspension or domain-level spam-folder routing; detection metric: Daily seed-list inbox placement (%) and bounce rate (<1.5% hard threshold); fallback: Enforce max 2–3 domains per tenant, strip all open/click tracking pixels, verify 100% of leads via SMTP catch-all checks before sending, and keep hot-standby warmed domains ready for instant swap;
